title: A Young Canyon in Ancient Rock
place: Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA
text: The Grand Canyon looks ancient, but the gorge itself is young. The Colorado River began cutting down only 5 to 6 million years ago, slicing through rocks far older than itself: the top layer is 270 million years old, and the inner gorge holds rocks about 1.8 billion years old. A steep slope, big floods and a dry climate let the river carve astonishingly fast.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service: Grand Canyon Geology

title: A Crater Hiding Under Chesapeake Bay
place: Lower Chesapeake Bay, near Cape Charles, Virginia, USA
text: About 35 million years ago, a space rock roughly 2 to 3 miles wide slammed into the shallow sea shelf off what is now Virginia. It blasted out a crater about 90 kilometres across, now buried under 1,000 to 1,500 feet of rubble and sea sediment beneath the lower Chesapeake Bay. USGS scientist Wylie Poag uncovered it using drill cores and seismic surveys of the seabed.

source.name: USGS: Chesapeake Bay Meteorite Impact Crater

source2.name: USGS Virginia and West Virginia Water Science Center: The Chesapeake Bay Impact Crater

title: Lava Rivers That Reached the Pacific
place: Rowena Crest, Columbia River Gorge, Oregon, USA
text: Beginning about 16.7 million years ago, long cracks in the ground of eastern Oregon, Washington and Idaho poured out more than 350 lava flows. Many single flows held over 1,000 cubic kilometres of molten rock, and some crossed the Cascades all the way to the Pacific Ocean. Piled up to 4,000 metres thick, the layers now line the Columbia River Gorge like pages in a giant book.

source.name: USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory: Columbia River Basalt Group Stretches from Oregon to Idaho

source2.name: U.S. National Park Service: Fissure Volcanoes

title: Forty Thousand Columns of Cooled Lava
place: Giant's Causeway, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, UK
text: About 60 million years ago, as the North Atlantic was beginning to open, lava flooded across what is now Northern Ireland. Thick flows cooled, shrank and cracked into some 40,000 tidy basalt columns, the stepping stones of the Giant's Causeway. New dating shows all of Northern Ireland's volcanic rocks formed in just 5.5 million years, eight million fewer than geologists once believed.

source.name: British Geological Survey: Scientists make new discovery in the history of the Giant's Causeway

title: The Continent That Sank Out of Sight
place: Zealandia, highest point Aoraki / Mount Cook, New Zealand
text: About 84 million years ago, a long ribbon of land tore away from the supercontinent Gondwana. It had been stretched thin before breaking free, so it sank: today about 94% of its 4.9 million square kilometres lies underwater. In 2017 geologists argued it is Earth's seventh continent, Zealandia, the youngest, thinnest and most submerged of all. New Zealand is among the few bits still above the waves.

source.name: GSA Today (Mortimer et al. 2017): Zealandia: Earth's Hidden Continent

title: How Old Is the Sahara?
place: Djurab Desert, northern Chad
text: When did the Sahara become a desert? Most scientists said 2 to 3 million years ago, but petrified sand dunes in Chad, dated by nearby fossils, hinted at about 7 million. In 2014 climate modellers offered a cause: the shrinking Tethys Sea, ancestor of the Mediterranean, weakened the monsoon rains reaching North Africa. Not everyone is convinced; one desert geologist called it "numerical speculation."

source.name: Science News: Shrinking ancient sea may have spawned Sahara Desert

title: The Flood That Refilled the Mediterranean
place: Malta Escarpment, Ionian Sea, off south-east Sicily, Italy
text: After the Mediterranean had partly dried out, the Atlantic came roaring back about 5.3 million years ago. Water spilling east through a gateway in south-eastern Sicily plunged into the eastern basin, whose surface may have sat up to 2,400 metres below today's sea level. Seismic surveys have found the leftover heap: up to 860 metres thick and over 1,400 cubic kilometres, perhaps Earth's largest megaflood deposit.

source.name: Scientific Reports (Micallef et al. 2018): Evidence of the Zanclean megaflood in the eastern Mediterranean Basin

title: Twin Craters That Weren't Twins
place: Nördlinger Ries, Bavaria, Germany
text: About 14.8 million years ago an asteroid blasted out the Nördlinger Ries, a crater about 24 kilometres wide in southern Germany. Only 40 kilometres away lies the much smaller Steinheim Basin, and for decades textbooks called them twins made by a split asteroid. But two separate earthquake-shaken layers in nearby sediments suggest Steinheim's impact came roughly half a million to 800,000 years later.

source.name: Scientific Reports (2022): Event- and biostratigraphic evidence for two independent Ries and Steinheim asteroid impacts in the Middle Miocene

title: Patagonia's Towers Were Born Underground
place: Torres del Paine National Park, Magallanes, Chile
text: The famous granite towers of Torres del Paine began as molten rock squeezed between layers 2 to 3 kilometres underground, about 12.5 million years ago. Precise dating shows the granite arrived in at least three batches, followed by dark sheets of mafic magma slipped in beneath, all within about 150,000 years, a blink in geological time. Erosion later stripped away the rock above and exposed the roof.

source.name: European Journal of Mineralogy (2020): Contact metamorphism and the assembly of the Torres del Paine intrusive complex

source2.name: University of Bristol Research: Time resolved construction of a bimodal laccolith (Torres del Paine, Patagonia)

title: Pebbles That Sat Still for Ages
place: Coastal Cordillera above Quebrada de Jazpampa, Atacama Desert, Chile
text: Quartz pebbles lying on flat ground in Chile's Atacama Desert have barely moved for tens of millions of years. By measuring neon made inside them by cosmic rays, scientists found 32 of 135 had sat at the surface since before the Miocene, one perhaps for 62 million years. They argue the desert's core turned hyperarid by the Mid to Late Eocene, as Earth cooled.

source.name: Nature Communications (2026): Evidence for Eocene aridification of the Atacama Desert's hyperarid core

title: A Tibetan Valley Climbs Two Kilometres
place: Meiduo Village, Luolong County, Tibet, China
text: Today the Luolong Basin in eastern Tibet sits 3,600 to 5,200 metres high. Yet between about 54 and 46 million years ago it lay only around 600 metres up, covered in dry scrub. By roughly 44 million years ago it had risen to about 2.9 kilometres, where palms, laurels, oaks and willows grew together. Scientists collected 2,387 fossils from that forest, including leaves, insects and fish.

source.name: National Science Review (2025): The raising and westward expansion of central Tibet

title: Scandinavian Boulders Reach the Netherlands
place: Molenweg quarry, Hattem, Gelderland, Netherlands
text: About 2.4 million years ago, a great ice sheet spread out of Scandinavia and carried boulders all the way to what is now the Netherlands. Granites from Åland and Finland and sandstones from Bornholm and Öland lie in gravels near the town of Hattem. New dating of these rocks shows Europe's first big ice sheet grew more than a million years earlier than once thought.

source.name: Nature Communications (2026): A continental-scale Eurasian ice sheet 2.4 million years ago

title: Arabia Starts Tearing Away from Africa
place: Tihama Asir complex, east of the Jizan coastal plain, Saudi Arabia
text: About 26 million years ago, Arabia was beginning to tear away from Africa. A mantle plume under Afar had weakened the crust, and magma flooded into it, leaving gabbros and dike swarms thousands of kilometres long beside today's Red Sea coast. A 2025 study argues this magma actually patched and thickened the stretching crust, delaying true seafloor spreading in the southern Red Sea until about 5 million years ago.

source.name: Nature Communications (2025): Magmatic underplating and crustal intrusions accommodate extension during Red Sea continental rifting

title: Cave Stones Remember a Wetter Arabia
place: As Sulb Plateau, central Saudi Arabia
text: Beneath the stony As Sulb Plateau of central Saudi Arabia, cave formations grow only when rain soaks the ground above. Dating stalagmites and flowstones from seven caves, with names like Hotel Cave and Mossy Cave, scientists found wet spells stretching back to 7.44 million years ago. Fossils of about the same age from the nearby UAE show crocodiles and hippos once lived in what is now desert.

source.name: Nature (2025): Recurrent humid phases in Arabia over the past 8 million years

title: The Aleutian Volcano Chain Is Born
place: Agattu Island forearc, western Aleutian Islands, Alaska, USA
text: About 56 million years ago or earlier, the Pacific seafloor began diving beneath what became the Aleutian Islands, a volcanic arc now nearly 4,000 kilometres long. Researchers dredged basalts from the seabed near Agattu Island and dated them to about 55.6 million years, far older than most earlier estimates. The change came as the whole Pacific Plate swung from heading west-northwest to heading north.

source.name: Nature Communications (2026): Tectonic and climatic implications of the Aleutian Arc initiation 56 million years ago

title: A Weak Start for Earth's Mightiest Current
place: Drake Passage, between South America and Antarctica
text: When Antarctica first froze over, about 33.7 million years ago, new ocean gaps had opened at the Tasman Gateway and Drake Passage. Yet climate simulations suggest the current circling Antarctica, today Earth's strongest, was still feeble. The gaps did not line up with the westerly winds, so the flow reached only about 35% of its pre-industrial strength, and a shallow seaway even cut off the Antarctic Peninsula.

source.name: PNAS (2026): Configuration of circum-Antarctic circulation at the last green- to icehouse climate transition

title: The Sharp Turn in Hawaii's Volcano Trail
place: Hawaiian-Emperor Bend, northwest Pacific Ocean
text: On the floor of the northwest Pacific, the trail of volcanoes left by the Hawaiian hotspot makes a sharp 60° turn, formed about 47 million years ago. For decades geologists argued over whether the Pacific Plate changed direction or the hotspot itself wandered. A 2025 computer study says both mattered: the hotspot drifted south and also west, and the westward drift alone adds about 20° to the bend.

source.name: PNAS (2025): Dynamics of longitudinal Hawaiian hotspot motion and the formation of the Hawaiian-Emperor Bend

title: Volcanoes That Took the Ocean's Breath
place: Mentelle Basin, off south-west Western Australia
text: About 94 million years ago, in a super-hot world with exceptionally high seas, oxygen ran short across much of the ocean. What set it off? Drill cores from the Mentelle Basin off Western Australia hold pulses of mercury, an element volcanoes release in vast amounts, just before and during the crisis. The likely culprit: huge eruptions building the Kerguelen Plateau in the southern Indian Ocean.

source.name: Nature Communications (2024): Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 triggered by Kerguelen volcanism

title: Why Turkana Dodged the Lava Floods
place: Turkana Depression, northern Kenya
text: Around 31 to 29 million years ago, one to two kilometres of lava piled up on the Ethiopian Plateau, fed by a plume of hot mantle rising beneath East Africa. Just to the south, the Turkana Depression sat on thin crust left by an older failed rift, an obvious weak spot. Yet seismic surveys show it largely escaped: its old rift had become drained and stiff, not weak.

source.name: Nature (2025): The importance of past rifting in large igneous province development

title: Rivers That Stole Their Way to Canyons
place: San Gabán Canyon, Puno, Peru
text: Along the northeastern edge of the high Andean Plateau in Peru, rivers have sawn canyons 2 to 3 kilometres deep, the largest being San Gabán. Modelling suggests the trick was capture: once mountain-building slowed after about 10 million years ago, rivers ate back into closed, inward-draining basins on the plateau and grabbed their water. Captures around 7 to 5 and 3.5 to 0.5 million years ago supercharged erosion.

source.name: Science Advances (2025): Drivers of canyon incision in the Peruvian Andes

title: Monsoon Secrets in Maldives Mud
place: Maldives Inner Sea (IODP Site U1467), Maldives
text: The Maldives' double row of atolls encloses a sheltered inner sea that rivers barely reach, so mostly windblown dust settles there. Drilling 708 metres into its mud, scientists traced dust from northeastern Africa and Arabia carried by summer monsoon winds. The record suggests the South Asian summer monsoon winds have weakened in two steps since about 12 million years ago, as ice sheets grew.

source.name: Nature Communications (2023): Weakening of the South Asian summer monsoon linked to interhemispheric ice-sheet growth since 12 Ma

title: Sea Algae Measure Tibet's Rise
place: Honggou section, Qaidam Basin, Qinghai, China
text: Tiny algae usually found only in the sea once lived in an ancient lake in the Qaidam Basin, on Tibet's northern edge, perhaps arriving with a Middle Miocene seawater incursion. Their fatty molecules record water temperature. They show the lake cooled by about 6.6°C in a geologically quick burst, either around 11 or 7.7 million years ago, meaning the basin rose roughly 1.5 kilometres.

source.name: Science Advances (2025): Terrestrial temperature history reveals Late Miocene rapid uplift of the northern Tibetan Plateau

title: Where the Loess Plateau's Red Dust Came From
place: Chaona section, Loess Plateau, Gansu, China
text: On China's Loess Plateau, reddish dust layers called the Red Clay were piling up by about 8 million years ago. Scientists long read them as a sign of inner Asia drying out. But dating tiny zircon crystals from the Chaona section showed much of the dust came from the Qilian Mountains and eastern lowlands, eroded by stronger summer monsoon rains. Meanwhile dust reaching the North Pacific rose about tenfold.

source.name: Science Advances (2018): Pre-Quaternary decoupling between Asian aridification and high dust accumulation rates

title: The Deep Door Between Two Oceans Shuts
place: Deep basin of the South China Sea (IODP drilling area)
text: Until about 10 million years ago, cold deep water from around Antarctica flowed from the Indian Ocean through gaps among the Indonesian islands into the deep South China Sea, piling up current-built sediment drifts on the seafloor. Drill cores and seismic images show that flow faded when the deep Indonesian Gateway finally closed, cutting the deep link between the Pacific and Indian Oceans and reshuffling global ocean circulation.

source.name: Nature Communications (2024): South China Sea records Late Miocene reorganization of western Pacific deep circulation

title: Malta's Cliffs Record a Cooling World
place: Ras il-Pellegrin, Malta
text: At Ras il-Pellegrin on Malta, the cliff layers change from Globigerina Limestone to Blue Clay. That switch, during a cooling step between about 14.7 and 12.8 million years ago when Antarctica's ice expanded, is the official global marker for the start of the Serravallian age. Chemistry in tiny shells shows the sea there then freshened in pulses, as stronger monsoon rains fell over North Africa.

source.name: Science Advances (2026): Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition
